items.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012
items.q: Cal Tjader was another one that inspired me, told me I should go to New York, it was Cal.

ctx.x: It’s like with the touch of a pianist. You can have Oscar Peterson sit at a Steinway and play a little bit, and then you’d have Dick Hyman do it, or Teddy Wilson or Billy Charlap, it’d all sound different. It’s the touch. And it’s the same with the mallet. Hampton used to play very softly but with very hard mallets. I use sort of a medium mallet, and at times I can be a little aggressive, because the music inspires you, you © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

know. I don’t like to play too hard because then there’s a limit as to how much volume you can get. But Hampton and I did a television show together. I had a television series I was the host of, and he came as a guest. And he played first of all, then we got together and we did “Seven Come Eleven” together. And I gave him my instrument and I had another instrument. He picked up my mallets. He started to play. That’s Lionel Hampton. You could hear it right away. Red Norvo was another one.
